title: The Indian-American Midterm Dilemma: A Community Pulled Between Prosperity and Immigration Crackdowns
excerpt: About 5.2 million Indian Americans — among America's highest-earning, best-educated communities — head into the November 3 midterms with legal immigration at the top of their concerns, just as the administration's PERM suspension and H-1B measures test their 2024 shift toward Republicans.
body:
• Indian Americans number about 5.2 million — the second-largest immigrant group in the US — with roughly three million voters for whom legal immigration is a high-priority issue.
  • Firstpost America reports new 2026 polling shows a sharp reversal of the gains Donald Trump made with Indian-American voters in 2024, with most now leaning Democratic.
  • The House's six-member informal "Samosa Caucus" is likely to shrink to four after November 3 unless Democrats Amish Shah in Arizona or Pia Dandiya in Florida win close races.
  • The administration's PERM suspension for major IT employers, the $100,000 H-1B fee and tighter work-permit rules are the policies most directly testing the community's allegiance.

Indian Americans have moved from the margins of US politics to the centre of its electoral conversation. At around 5.2 million, the community is America's second-largest immigrant group and among its highest-earning and best-educated — and as President Donald Trump faces the first major electoral test of his second term, its votes could prove important in several closely contested races, according to analysis published this week by The Hindu BusinessLine and Firstpost's Inside America coverage.

The dilemma is structural. The community's economic profile pulled a meaningful share of its voters toward Republicans in 2024. Since then, the administration's immigration agenda has landed on precisely the programmes Indian families use: the Labor Department's suspension of PERM green card processing for Microsoft and top Indian IT companies, the $100,000 H-1B fee, and this week's final rule ending automatic work-permit extensions for H-4 spouses. Firstpost America reports that new 2026 polling suggests Indian-American support has sharply reversed, with most voters now leaning toward Democrats, driven by economic pressures, immigration policies, concerns over racism, and strained US-India relations.

The representation stakes

Before 2012, only two Indian Americans had served in Congress — Dalip Singh Saund of California (1957-1963) and Bobby Jindal of Louisiana (2005-2008). Ami Bera's 2012 election began a steady rise: Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal and Raja Krishnamoorthi arrived in 2017, Shri Thanedar in 2023 and Suhas Subramanyam in 2025. All six current members — the informal "Samosa Caucus" — are Democrats.

This year the pattern may pause. The number of Indian Americans in the House is likely to fall from six to four after the November 3 polls, with Krishnamoorthi and Thanedar preparing to leave the chamber, unless Democrats Amish Shah in Arizona or Pia Dandiya in Florida win their closely fought races. The caucus is unlikely to grow beyond six in January, as no other Indian American is a competitive House nominee; Republicans Ritesh Tandon, Nirav Sheth and Mahesh Ganorkar are running in solidly Democratic seats.

The other side's case — and the warning from within

The administration's defenders frame the immigration measures as worker protection. Vice President JD Vance, defending the PERM action, argued employers cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign workers. New Delhi called the statement "unwarranted and deeply offensive," responding that America has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour and enterprise contributed to its prosperity.

The Hindu BusinessLine's Washington analysis notes the political risk cuts the other way: the PERM move may have been welcomed by the MAGA base, but even some Republicans are questioning the timing, and whether alienating three million Indian-American voters — concentrated in key suburban centres and animated by legal immigration — was a smart thing to do, particularly as Hispanic and African American voters who powered Trump's 2024 win are also moving away in large numbers. The irony was not lost on observers that on the same day, Trump honoured Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and five other tech leaders with national medals — five of the six awardees born outside the US.

What to watch

Turnout is the community's leverage: Indian-American voter turnout intentions are exceptionally high, and in marginal suburban House districts a motivated bloc of this size can decide outcomes. The Shah and Dandiya races, and whether the Samosa Caucus holds at four or recovers to six, will be the clearest scoreboard on November 3.
